757.title: the Rajasuya
757.hook: the kings arrive with gifts, the fire is lit, and everyone at Indraprastha is handed a job
757.carry: where you stand changes what you see
757.howItsDone: Some retellings of the Sabha Parva hold up Krishna washing the Brahmins' feet at the Rajasuya as a picture of humility in service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four brothers rode to the four directions for the Rajasuya, and at the northern gate Arjuna asked instead of forcing his way. Ask instead of pushing.

The hall at Indraprastha is crowded. Kings have come from near and far, and none came empty-handed: jewels, fine cloth, horses, gold, things the poem names one after another. Priests tend the sacred fire. Food goes out by the basketful. And among the guests are the cousins from Hastinapura, Duryodhana and his brothers, not rivals today but family with work to do. After all the planning, the Rajasuya itself is underway. The question is where each person is standing.
screen: `A HALL FULL OF KINGS.` → `GIFTS BEYOND COUNTING.` → `THE COUSINS ARE HERE TOO.`

segments.voice: A rite this big needs hands, so Yudhishthira hands out jobs. In the telling, the elders Bhishma and Drona watch over everything. Kripa is put in charge of the wealth. Vidura looks after the spending. Duhshasana sees to the food. And Duryodhana is given the task of receiving the gifts the kings bring. Picture it: every jewel, every horse, every bolt of silk meant for his cousin passes through his own hands first. Now look across the hall. The poem says that Krishna, the honored friend, chose a humble job of his own: washing the feet of the Brahmins who had come. The guest the whole family honors is kneeling with a basin of water. On paper, the Rajasuya is a consecration. The kings who bring gifts are saying, in effect, we recognize you as sovereign: a public yes, said with gold. Yudhishthira is the center of it. But a great gathering is never only about the person at the center. It's every person working around the edges, and what they feel while they do it. Krishna is at the edge by choice, and seems at peace there. Duryodhana is at the edge by assignment, counting someone else's wealth. Same rite, very different views. Hold onto Duryodhana at that gift table; the poem isn't finished with him. And not every king in the hall is happy about who's being honored. One of them is about to say so out loud.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a gathering you were part of, a wedding, a holiday meal, a big day at work, and find your own place in it, not the person at the center. What job did you have, and did you choose it, or was it handed to you? If you pray, you can offer that small job, and whoever you served, in your prayer; if not, simply rest with the memory.
The Rajasuya. A royal consecration where kings bring gifts as a sign of recognition, and where everyone, from Krishna to Duryodhana, has a part to play.
Your line: where you stand changes what you see. Krishna and Duryodhana stood in the same hall. Day seven hundred fifty-seven, done.

758.title: Shishupala
758.hook: the rite needs someone to receive the first honor, Bhishma names Krishna, and the king of Chedi stands up
758.carry: wait one breath before you say anything
758.howItsDone: Offering arghya, water and a respectful welcome to an honored guest or to a deity, is part of traditional Hindu hospitality and worship; at the Rajasuya, the Mahabharata turns the whole scene on who receives it first.

segments.voice: Yesterday at the Rajasuya, Duryodhana received the gifts and Krishna washed the guests' feet. Where you stand changes what you see.
screen: `WHERE YOU STAND CHANGES WHAT YOU SEE.`

segments.voice: Who gets served first? It sounds small until you're the host: the seating plan, the first plate, the toast. At Yudhishthira's great rite, the question has a name. The custom is to offer an honored guest the arghya, a respectful welcome of water and gifts, and one guest must receive it first, before all the others. The hall is full of kings, elders, teachers and priests. Whoever is chosen, someone else is not. And one man will not accept the answer.
screen: `WHO IS SERVED FIRST?` → `THE ARGHYA: THE GUEST'S WELCOME.` → `ONE CHOSEN, MANY NOT.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira turns to the eldest of the family, his grandfather Bhishma: who should receive the first honor? Bhishma doesn't name a king or a priest. He names Krishna. In the telling, he says that among all those gathered, Krishna shines like the sun among lights. So the youngest Pandava, Sahadeva, brings the arghya and offers it to Krishna, and Krishna accepts it. That should be the end of it: chosen by the eldest, offered by the host, received by the guest. But a voice rises from the crowd. It belongs to Shishupala, king of Chedi, and he is furious. Two things to know about him. First, he isn't a stranger. Shishupala is Krishna's cousin, the son of Krishna's father's sister, and the poem will show later that the bond between them runs strange and deep. Second, he doesn't object quietly or take Yudhishthira aside. He stands up in front of every king in the hall and makes his complaint as public as the honor was. That's this week: an honor given in public, and an objection that refuses to stay small. Over the next days we'll hear what he says, how the hall answers, and why Krishna waits so long before he answers at all.

segments.voice: Think of a time someone else was honored and you weren't: a promotion, a prize, a toast, a seat at the head of the table. Don't judge the feeling that comes; just notice where it lives in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach, and breathe into that spot slowly, a few times. If you pray, you can bring that moment into your prayer; if not, let the breath soften it a little.

759.title: Shishupala
759.hook: Shishupala makes his case against Krishna's honor, and Yudhishthira goes after him with gentle words
759.carry: one gentle sentence before a sharp one
759.howItsDone: Some Hindus who read or hear the Sabha Parva discuss this scene as a lesson in a host's duty to guests and in how to answer insult, with Yudhishthira's gentleness and Bhishma's firmness both part of the conversation.

segments.voice: Yesterday we met Shishupala, king of Chedi, rising as Krishna received the first honor. Wait one breath before you say anything.

Shishupala has the floor, and he isn't shouting nonsense. That's what makes this scene uncomfortable. He's built an argument, point by point, and he delivers it to a hall full of kings. If you wanted to honor age, there are elders here. If you wanted to honor a teacher, there's a teacher here. If you wanted to honor a king, Krishna isn't even a crowned king. So why him? It's the kind of speech that makes a room shift in its seats.
screen: `NOT NONSENSE: AN ARGUMENT.` → `NOT THE ELDEST, NOT THE TEACHER.` → `NOT EVEN A CROWNED KING.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shishupala goes through the room like a lawyer. He names the honored elders sitting right there: the great teacher Drona, the sage Vyasa, Bhishma himself. Any of them, he says, had a better claim than Krishna. Then the argument turns into insult. The Pandavas have shamed themselves, he says, and Krishna has shamed himself by accepting what wasn't his. With that he gets up to leave, and some of the kings stir with him. Now watch Yudhishthira. It's his great day, and his choice has just been mocked in front of everyone. He doesn't send a guard or answer insult with insult. He goes after Shishupala himself and speaks to him gently, in effect: this is not a fitting way to speak, Bhishma knows what is right, and the other kings have accepted the choice. A host trying to keep a guest at the table. Then Bhishma speaks, far less softly. Someone who won't accept honoring Krishna, he says, doesn't need to be coaxed. Two answers to the same insult, side by side: the host reaches out, the elder holds firm. The poem lets both stand, and lets Shishupala's anger keep growing between them. And through all of it, Krishna hasn't said a word.
screen: `SHISHUPALA NAMES THE ELDERS.` · `THE ARGUMENT TURNS TO INSULT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA SPEAKS GENTLY.` · `BHISHMA HOLDS FIRM.` · then, large: `KRISHNA SAYS NOTHING.`

760.title: Shishupala
760.hook: the angry kings gather around Shishupala, Bhishma speaks of a sleeping lion, and Bhima has to be held back
760.howItsDone: In some retellings of the Sabha Parva, Bhishma restraining Bhima, even while Shishupala mocks him, is told as a picture of an elder's self-control.

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala made his case and walked out, and Yudhishthira followed him with gentle words. One gentle sentence before a sharp one.

A room can turn in a few seconds. One person's anger becomes a murmur, the murmur becomes a group, and the group starts talking about a fight. That's where the Rajasuya is now. Other kings have gathered around Shishupala, and in the telling they begin to talk of war, of spoiling the rite before it's finished. Yudhishthira, the host, is worried, and he turns again to his grandfather. Two kinds of anger in one hall: the kind that spreads, and the kind that has to be held back.
screen: `ONE ANGER BECOMES A CROWD.` → `TALK OF WAR AT THE RITE.` → `THE HOST IS WORRIED.`

segments.voice: First, the youngest Pandava speaks up. Sahadeva, who carried the arghya to Krishna, dares anyone who objects to the honor to answer him. Nobody does. Then Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what to do about the kings. Bhishma isn't troubled. He gives an image instead of a plan: these kings are like dogs barking around a sleeping lion, and the lion hasn't woken up yet. A striking thing to say about a room full of crowned rulers. Shishupala turns his anger on Bhishma. He mocks the old man with a little fable about a bird that preaches caution while picking scraps of meat from a lion's teeth: that's Bhishma, all fine words and no courage. He mocks the stories told about Krishna's childhood, too. That's when Bhima rises. The poem describes his rage as terrible to see, his eyes blazing, ready to spring at Shishupala. And Bhishma, the very man being insulted, holds him back and calms him down. So look at the hall. Shishupala's anger keeps spreading, pulling in kings, reaching for anyone nearby. Bhima's is just as hot, but it's caught and held by an elder who takes the insult and refuses to let it become a brawl. And Krishna, the sleeping lion in Bhishma's picture, still hasn't moved.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that made you angry recently, and let yourself feel a little of it: the heat, the quickening. Don't push it away; hold it the way a hand rests on a friend's shoulder, and breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in, a few times. If you pray, you can bring that anger into your prayer just as it is; if not, simply keep breathing with it.

761.title: Shishupala
761.hook: Bhishma tells the hall how Shishupala was born, and why Krishna once promised his mother a hundred pardons
761.carry: his silence is a promise kept
761.howItsDone: Some storytellers and commentators use Shishupala's birth story to explain Krishna's patience in the hall, reading his silence as the keeping of a promise to his aunt.

segments.voice: Yesterday Shishupala's anger spread through the hall, Bhishma held Bhima back, and Krishna still hadn't moved. One long breath out first.
screen: `ANGER THAT SPREADS, ANGER THAT IS HELD.`

segments.voice: The kings are muttering about war. Bhima has nearly leapt across the hall. Bhishma has been mocked to his face. And the one person all of this is about just sits there, and hasn't said a word. So Bhishma, still holding Bhima's arm, does something unexpected. He stops the argument and tells a story. If you want to understand this hall, he says in effect, you have to go back to the day Shishupala was born.
screen: `WHY IS KRISHNA SILENT?` → `BHISHMA TELLS A STORY.` → `BACK TO THE CRADLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Bhishma tells it. Shishupala was born in the royal house of Chedi with three eyes and four arms, and he cried out at birth with a strange, unearthly cry. His frightened parents thought of giving him up. Then a voice came from no one they could see. Don't abandon him. He will grow strong. His death is not yet. And it told them how to know who would end his life: the one on whose lap the child's extra arms would fall away and his third eye would vanish. So the king and queen put the baby on the lap of every visitor. King after king held him. Nothing happened. Then Krishna came to visit his aunt, and the child was placed on his lap. The two extra arms fell away. The third eye sank into his forehead and was gone. Now his mother knew whose hand would one day take her son's life, and she was Krishna's father's sister. She begged him for a boon: spare my son. Krishna promised to pardon a hundred of Shishupala's offenses, even ones that deserved death. So that's what Krishna is doing in the hall. He isn't ignoring the insults. He's counting them. His silence is a promise to his aunt, made over a cradle long ago, kept insult by insult. Patience here isn't the absence of anger. It's a word given, and honored, even when it costs something.
screen: `THREE EYES AND FOUR ARMS.` · `A VOICE: DON'T ABANDON HIM.` · `ON KRISHNA'S LAP, THE SIGNS FALL AWAY.` · `A MOTHER ASKS, KRISHNA PROMISES.` · then, large: `HIS SILENCE IS A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise you're keeping, maybe quietly and for a long time: to call, to show up, to be patient with someone who's hard to be patient with. See the person you made it to; breathe in and feel the weight of it, breathe out and notice what keeping it has asked of you. If you pray, you can hold that promise in your prayer; if not, simply honor it in silence.

762.title: Shishupala
762.hook: Shishupala challenges Krishna to fight, and Krishna finally speaks: the pardons are used up
762.carry: name your limit, kindly and clearly
762.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings and devotional art, the Sudarshana discus is one of Krishna's signs, and some tellers present the end of Shishupala as the moment his long patience reaches its promised limit.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma told of Shishupala's birth, and Krishna's promise to his aunt: a hundred pardons. His silence is a promise kept.

Bhishma's story should have cooled the room. It does the opposite. Shishupala hears that he's been spared all his life by Krishna's promise, and he isn't grateful. He's insulted. He turns from Bhishma to Krishna himself and calls him out: stand up and fight me. For the first time in this whole scene, the challenge is aimed straight at the silent guest, with every king watching. And after all that waiting, Krishna speaks.
screen: `THE STORY DOESN'T COOL HIM.` → `FIGHT ME.` → `THE SILENT GUEST STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer Shishupala first. He turns to the kings. In the telling, he lays out what Shishupala has done: wrongs against Krishna's own people, some of them while Krishna was far away and couldn't defend them. He reminds the hall that Shishupala is his aunt's son, and that for her sake he has borne all of it. Then comes the line the whole week has waited for, in effect: the hundred are full. The promise has been kept to the end. Shishupala doesn't back down. He laughs at Krishna and dares him to do his worst. So Krishna calls to mind his discus, the spinning weapon that is his in the stories, and it comes to his hand. In front of all the kings, he strikes, and the king of Chedi falls. The order matters. Krishna doesn't strike at the first insult, or the tenth, or when Bhima wants to. He waits until his word to his aunt has been fully kept, and even then he explains himself to the room first. Patience and judgment are two parts of the same thing here. Patience has a shape and a limit, and the limit was set long ago, in love, for a frightened mother. Some readers find the ending hard. Some find it just. The poem gives us the waiting, the warning and the blow, and lets us hold all three.

763.howItsDone: In some devotional traditions, the end of Shishupala is told as a teaching that even hatred, if it fixes the mind on Krishna, can bring a person to him; other readers take a different meaning, and the Mahabharata itself does not explain the light.

segments.voice: Shishupala has fallen, and the hall is silent. But the poem isn't done with him. Something rises from his body: a radiance, the text says, bright as the sun. Every eye in the hall follows it. It moves toward Krishna, bows to him, and enters him. The man who railed against Krishna in front of every king ends inside him. It's a strange ending, and the poem says the kings who saw it were amazed.
screen: `A LIGHT RISES FROM HIS BODY.` → `IT BOWS TO KRISHNA.` → `IT ENTERS HIM.`

segments.voice: What does it mean that Shishupala's light enters Krishna? The poem shows it and moves on, so readers have filled the space. Some Hindus, especially in devotional traditions, read it this way: Shishupala thought about Krishna constantly, even if every thought was hatred, and that fierce, single-minded attention brought him to Krishna in the end. Others read it more simply: everything that lives returns, at last, to its source. The text doesn't settle it, and i won't either. Then the story turns practical. Yudhishthira, the host, has the funeral rites performed for Shishupala, and places Shishupala's son on the throne of Chedi. The fallen king's line keeps its crown. The rite is finished, the guests are honored and sent home, and Krishna returns to his own city. Look back at the week. The Rajasuya, with everyone handed a job: Krishna washing feet, Duryodhana receiving the gifts. Bhishma named Krishna for the first honor, and Shishupala stood up. He made his case, and Yudhishthira answered with gentleness. The kings grew angry; Bhishma spoke of a sleeping lion, and held Bhima back. Then the cradle and a promise of a hundred pardons, the limit and the discus, and now the light. Shishupala's story ends here. But remember the cousin at the gift table. He's still in Indraprastha, and the next story is his.
